The glasschord is a struck glass idiophone designed around 1785 by the Paris physicist M. Beyer; the French name is fortepiano à cordes de verre, and its form is close to that of the celesta. It sounds when cloth-wrapped wooden mallets strike glass tubes resting on strips of cloth, has no damper, and the usual models have a range of about three octaves. Franklin gave it its name, and the idea behind it was inspired by the glass harmonica he had made. The instrument appears in scores such as the first version of Berlioz's La Tempête and Saint-Saëns's L'aquarium.

玻璃弦琴約於1785年由巴黎物理學家貝耶發明，屬敲擊式玻璃體鳴樂器，外形近似鋼片: The glasschord was invented around 1785 by the Paris physicist Beyer. It is a struck glass idiophone and looks rather like a celesta. It sounds when cloth-wrapped wooden mallets strike glass tubes laid on strips of cloth; it has no damper, and its range is about three octaves, different models running from c' to c'', from f' to f'' or from g' to g''. Beyer showed the still unnamed instrument at the French Academy of Sciences on 19 January 1785, and the Journal de Paris reported it several times that year. It was inspired by Franklin's glass harmonica and named by Franklin; on 6 July 1785 Jefferson recorded that Franklin had brought a version with him. In the early nineteenth century the Chappell company made it in quantity until about 1815, and it later appears in the first version of Berlioz's La Tempête and in Saint-Saëns's L'aquarium.
玻璃弦琴音色清澈透亮，具有玻璃特有的脆性與晶瑩質感，敲擊時發出清脆悅耳的音響。其: The glasschord's timbre is clear and transparent, with the brittleness and glitter peculiar to glass; struck, it gives a bright, sweet sound. Its range is wide, from warm and heavy in the low register to bright and piercing at the top, with clear layers between. Because the sounding bodies are glass, the resonance is unusual: the natural vibration of the glass gives the tone a lustre of its own, so the sound has the purity of a crystal tuning fork. Compared with the metallic quality of the celesta, the glasschord is softer and more elegant; compared with the glass harmonica its tone is more penetrating and more directional. After the strike the sound decays quickly, with a short, clear envelope, which suits light, transparent textures, and it is often used in creative and experimental music.
